choices.text: A pericyclic cyclization of a conjugated acyclic polyene in which one π bond breaks and a new σ bond forms
A reaction in which two unsaturated molecules add to each other to give a ring
choices.why: That is a cycloaddition (Section 30.5). An electrocyclic reaction involves a single polyene.

choices.text: The migration of a σ-bonded group across a π electron system
choices.why: That is a sigmatropic rearrangement (Section 30.7).

choices.text: A ring closure in which a nucleophile attacks a carbocation in the same molecule
choices.why: Electrocyclic reactions are pericyclic, not polar: bonds reorganize in one step through a cyclic transition state.

explanation: An electrocyclic reaction is a pericyclic process that cyclizes a conjugated acyclic polyene. One π bond is broken, the other π bonds change position, a new σ bond is formed, and a cyclic compound results.

prompt: A conjugated triene (three C=C bonds) undergoes electrocyclic ring-closure to a cyclohexadiene. How many π bonds does the product have?
explanation: In an electrocyclic reaction one π bond is broken and a new σ bond forms; the other π bonds just change position. Three π bonds minus one leaves two, as in 1,3-cyclohexadiene.

prompt: What kind of ring does the electrocyclic ring-closure of a conjugated diene give?

choices.why: A cyclohexadiene comes from the ring-closure of a conjugated triene.
One π bond survives the ring-closure, so the ring keeps a double bond: a cyclobutene.
A cyclohexene comes from a Diels–Alder reaction of a diene with a dienophile, not from a diene alone.

explanation: A conjugated diene can be converted into a cyclobutene, and a conjugated triene into a cyclohexadiene. In each case one π bond becomes a new σ bond.

prompt: Pericyclic reactions are reversible. Where do the two electrocyclic equilibria in Section 30.2 generally lie?

choices.text: Triene ⇄ cyclohexadiene favors the ring; diene ⇄ cyclobutene favors the open-chain diene

choices.why: The diene ⇄ cyclobutene equilibrium favors the less strained open-chain diene.
The triene ⇄ cyclohexadiene equilibrium favors the cyclic product.

choices.text: Triene ⇄ cyclohexadiene favors the triene; diene ⇄ cyclobutene favors the cyclobutene
choices.why: This is the reverse. The strained four-membered ring is the one that is disfavored.

explanation: In general the triene ⇄ cyclohexadiene equilibrium favors the cyclic product, whereas the diene ⇄ cyclobutene equilibrium favors the less strained open-chain product.

prompt: What is the product when (2E,4Z,6E)-2,4,6-octatriene is heated?

choices.why: The trans product forms from this triene only under photochemical conditions, or thermally from the 2E,4Z,6Z isomer.

choices.text: A mixture of cis- and trans-5,6-dimethyl-1,3-cyclohexadiene
choices.why: Electrocyclic reactions are stereospecific: this triene gives only one isomer on heating.
A triene closes to a six-membered ring, a cyclohexadiene, not a cyclobutene.

explanation: Heating (2E,4Z,6E)-2,4,6-octatriene gives only cis-5,6-dimethyl-1,3-cyclohexadiene (Figure 30.2.1). The stereochemistry is the most striking feature of electrocyclic reactions.

prompt: What is the product when (2E,4Z,6Z)-2,4,6-octatriene is heated?

choices.why: The cis product comes from heating the 2E,4Z,6E isomer. Changing one terminal double bond changes the product.

choices.text: A mixture of cis- and trans-5,6-dimethyl-1,3-cyclohexadiene
choices.why: The reaction is stereospecific and gives a single isomer.
A cyclohexene would need two π bonds to become σ bonds. Electrocyclic ring-closure breaks only one, so the product is a cyclohexadiene.

explanation: (2E,4Z,6Z)-2,4,6-Octatriene yields only trans-5,6-dimethyl-1,3-cyclohexadiene when heated, whereas the 2E,4Z,6E isomer gives the cis product.

prompt: What is the product when (2E,4Z,6E)-2,4,6-octatriene is irradiated with ultraviolet light (hν)?

choices.why: That is the thermal product. Under photochemical conditions the stereochemical result changes completely.

choices.text: No reaction; electrocyclic reactions need heat
choices.why: Electrocyclic reactions occur under both thermal and photochemical conditions.

choices.text: A mixture of cis and trans products
choices.why: The photochemical reaction is also stereospecific; it gives the trans isomer.

explanation: Heating (2E,4Z,6E)-2,4,6-octatriene gives the cis product, but irradiation with UV light gives trans-5,6-dimethyl-1,3-cyclohexadiene (Figure 30.2.1).

prompt: Which diene does trans-3,4-dimethylcyclobutene give when heated?

choices.why: (2E,4Z)-2,4-Hexadiene comes from heating the cis isomer of 3,4-dimethylcyclobutene.
The ring-opening is stereospecific: the trans isomer gives only one diene.
Opening the cyclobutene ring breaks the σ bond between carbons 3 and 4 and gives a diene, keeping the two methyl groups.

explanation: The trans isomer of 3,4-dimethylcyclobutene yields only (2E,4E)-2,4-hexadiene when heated, and the cis isomer yields only (2E,4Z)-2,4-hexadiene (Figure 30.2.2).

prompt: Which diene does cis-3,4-dimethylcyclobutene give when heated?

choices.why: Heating gives (2E,4E)-2,4-hexadiene from the trans isomer. The cis isomer gives it only on UV irradiation.
The thermal product of the cis isomer has one E and one Z double bond.

choices.text: A mixture of all three 2,4-hexadiene isomers
choices.why: Thermal ring-opening is stereospecific and gives a single isomer.

explanation: cis-3,4-Dimethylcyclobutene yields only (2E,4Z)-2,4-hexadiene when heated. On UV irradiation the results are opposite (Figure 30.2.2).

prompt: For a bond to form at the ends of a polyene, the outermost lobes of like sign must meet. If those like-sign lobes are on opposite sides of the molecule, how must the two terminal orbitals rotate?

choices.text: In the same direction (both clockwise or both counterclockwise): conrotatory
In opposite directions (one clockwise, one counterclockwise): disrotatory
choices.why: Opposite-direction rotation is needed when lobes of like sign are on the same side of the molecule.
Conrotatory means both orbitals rotate in the same direction.

choices.text: They don't need to rotate; like-sign lobes overlap directly
choices.why: The outermost lobes must rotate so a positive lobe meets a positive lobe, or a negative meets a negative.

explanation: If lobes of like sign are on the same side, the orbitals rotate in opposite directions, one clockwise and one counterclockwise (disrotatory). If they are on opposite sides, both rotate in the same direction (conrotatory).
